Title: Ep. 78, Equity by Design: How Diversity Ignites Creativity
Video URL: https://youtu.be/39-kYM48a0Q
Categories: BUSINESS
Transcript:
[MUSIC] There is one catalyst that can amplify your organization's creativity and ignite its impact. Today, we will talk about the importance and value of diversity in our social networks. I'm Matt Abrahams, and I teach strategic communication at Stanford Graduate School of Business. Welcome to Think Fast, Talk Smart, The Podcast. [MUSIC] Today I am super excited to be joined by Adina Sterling, who is an associate professor of organizational behavior at Stanford GSB. Adina studies the causes and consequences of human relationships in organizations and markets. And she teaches a popular elective class called Equity by Design, and runs a lab by the same name. Welcome Adina, I'm super excited to get a chance to talk with you. >> Thanks, Matt, it's great to be here. >> Yes, well, thanks for being here. So let's go ahead and get started. A lot of your work focuses on social networks. For many of us, social networks refer to applications like Facebook, or Twitter, and LinkedIn. What do you mean by social networks and what types of insights can you learn from them? >> Right, so that's a great question to begin with. And you're absolutely right, we hear social networks and we think about Facebook, and LinkedIn, and Instagram, and things that 12 and 13 year olds are more savvy at, than we are. >> Yeah. >> So, what they are, are the patterns of interactions and communication that happens between various entities. So social scientists will study social networks that occur between individuals, between groups, between teams, between societies, organizations, institutions. And so social networks is a construct that travels different levels, and levels of analyses. And we care about them because a lot of the outcomes that individuals, groups, and organizations experience, have to do with the social networks that they have, where they are within this pattern of relationships. And so oftentimes we get a lot of our social resources from social networks, and so they can be awfully important. >> I see, so a social network is essentially a way of mapping the different connections and relationships we have within groupings of people. >> That's right. >> As you know, Adina, this podcast focuses a lot on communication. So I'm wondering, what role does communication play within social networks? And have you been able to determine any best practices that organizations use to maximize the impact of communication within their networks? So communication in the social networks are foundational to why social networks exist. So if I can't communicate effectively to you or you to me, our social tie goes away. So a lot of the way that we understand social ties is the transfer of information, advice, care, social support, and of course being able to communicate those aspects of life effectively. So the care that somebody would express to another depends on their ability to communicate that in a way that's empathetic and real. And so communication is foundational to social networks. What can organizations do to help employees communicate and help employees communicate with clients and other stakeholders? I always hear, Matt, go back to the importance of culture. So if the organization can put into place the right norms, the right expectations, the right language so that people can communicate, and they sort of know where the boundaries are, and where not to cross boundaries. Those can be really helpful ways of helping employees communicate their wants and needs, their ideas to one another and to other stakeholders. >> Wow, so I just learned that I've been a social networking- >> You have. >> Researcher for all these years, and I didn't know that that's what I was. No, that's great. So, thank you for sharing that the communication is absolutely critical in understanding social networks. And it sounds like organizations that put a priority on helping people communicate, the value of communication, and allowing people to feel that notion we've talked about before on this podcast of psychological safety, to feel comfortable communicating- >> That's right. >> Can be much more effective. >> Do you mind if I add one there? >> Please, yeah. >> Piece to what organizations can do, what you just teed up made me think of this. Another important part of communication that organizations can tap into is the notion that it can be multifaceted. So verbal communication, of course, is one way of communicating, auditory communication, but it's not the only way. And so, especially organizations that recognize neurodiversity, for example, will do things in a team setting like take pauses, give people think time. Allow people to write down ideas in the middle of a meeting, so that people's natural strengths, because we all have different strengths, don't all dominate, so that only certain people don't get to communicate their ideas. Organizations that do this well, collect ideas from many different people and allow for communication to come through many different mediums. >> I love that idea and it brings us really nicely into my next set of questions around what you teach in your Equity by Design class, and in the lab that you run. So it's really important from what I'm hearing you say that organizations don't just lock into one way of communicating, that they be very open to multiple ways, and they put a priority on communication. I will often recommend that organizations take time to reflect on their communication at the end of meetings, or one-on-one interaction, spend a few minutes just talking about the quality of the communication, not rehashing what was said, necessarily. And also as part of performance reviews and other big meetings, talk about communication and what you add so nicely to it is, it's not just one monolithic thing, there are lots of different ways to communicate. And we want to make sure that everybody can bring their best selves to the communication. Can you share with us some of the concepts you teach in your Equity by Design class, as well as the topics you study in your Equity by Design lab, what role does communication play in these efforts? >> Sure, so my class, as you mentioned, is on diversity, equity, and inclusion. And those are really three different ideas. In thinking about the importance of communication, it is awfully important for diversity. So let me say a little more about this. >> Please. >> We've now had several decades of work done by social scientists on what diversity buys you, what is the diversity bonus? Has been the question. And when people from different backgrounds that have different ideas come together, what research has shown is that they tend to outperform from a creativity and innovation standpoint, groups that are more homogeneous. But the key to having those benefits come about, is the ability for people to be able to communicate. So you could have a really diverse group- >> Right. >> And if everybody shuts down and nobody's communicating, it becomes really hard to build off of each other's ideas, to have those creative breakthroughs. You need people to be willing to share their thoughts and their ideas. And so that's one way communication is really key. >> The importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion are critical for many aspects of an organization for sure, and I'm curious to hear even more. So, first before we go, why better practices and not best practices? >> Okay, so that is a good question. The reason is that when it comes to this topic, what I found is that sometimes the great can be the enemy of the good. And so when I first began teaching this topic at Stanford, I had people say to me, my gosh, one of the things I'd like about your class is that we're taught to incrementally, just get going, right? We don't have to have the perfect plan for diversity, equity, and inclusion. What we can do is begin and have better practices from where we're at. So anyway, it's the idea of that the great shouldn't be the enemy of the good. >> I love it. I'm calling them better practices. >> Better practices, that's right. >> All right, what are some from your class? >> Yeah, so one important one is to understand that because diversity has benefits, sometimes you need to do things differently as a leader. The thing that diversity really helps you with is sometimes slowing down to take the time to be creative, to make better choices and have better solutions. So, there was this terrific study done that was actually looking at juries. And they found, these researchers, that juries that were more do diverse, they were more deliberate. People came more prepared and better able to argue their ideas, and outcomes generally reviewed as being better when there are these more diverse groups. And so the first, really it's about buying in [LAUGH] and understanding that it might take a little bit longer to build a diverse team, but that has some benefits in the long run. >> So taking the time and being thoughtful about putting the team together and then giving the team space to actually leverage the diverse perspectives that they bring can be really helpful. >> That's right, that's right. >> A lot of business is so much about rushing and being first and fast. >> That's right. >> And it sounds like what I'm hearing you say is sometimes being more deliberate and slowing down can give you an advantage as well. >> Yes. >> Great. >> Yeah, and then also building up the right culture around the team becomes key. >> Right, so that helping people feel connected and safe and that their voice has value. >> Exactly. >> Yeah, great, many of those listening into our podcast today worked for organizations that are in various stages of implementing their DE&I programs, based on your experience what are some of the best ways to implement, assess, and reinforce these programs? >> Sure, so I'd like to say if you can get by in from the top oftentimes there are grassroots efforts within organizations that are terrific around DEI and leadership can feel as though they're responding to DEI efforts. The other concept I would just add here is that I do like to talk about within organizations, what do you think of as. So we all think about innovation and going to be at the bleeding edge. The analogy doesn't quite work the same way. But traditionally, there are more marginalized groups within organizations. And so sometimes, sitting with and taking the temperature of those groups and figuring out how to implement policy changes that are affected there, can have enormous spillover effects for everyone. So, for example, if an organization goes on and surveys all recent parents for mothers, fathers, and the like about time off policies. They'll hear a lot of things in there that could also help older individuals that are taking care of their parents, Individuals that have family that are further away. And so organizations, that sit and listen to more marginalized groups, often times can use those insights, and blow them out and, and have effective policies for multiple groups within organizations. >> That's really, really fantastic. It's starts with listening, and then collaboration, and it has to come, not just from the grassroots, but also from the top and, and that's what leads to success. More and more as I do these podcasts, the role of listening, and taking the time to hear what others are saying is really a key ingredient to success in many aspects. And it sounds like DE&I is no different. I wanted to address another area of your research that I found really fascinating. You've identified something you term the confidence gap as a potential contributor to gender differences we see in the workplace, such as equity and pay. Can you explain what the confidence gap is, and how can it be addressed? >> Sure, so I'm glad we're chatting about this because sometimes the confidence gap can be misunderstood. So, I'll first explain it and then talk about where it comes from because that's a real key to this. So, the confidence gap, that idea came from a study that I and some researchers here at Stanford did where we tracked the outcomes of college students in engineering programs at 27 institutions. And it was a longitudinal study, so we were interested in people's, what we called self-efficacy, how much confidence they had in their ability to do engineering and stem and mathematics type problems early on, how that changed over time, where they were with respect to self-efficacy as they were entering the workplace, and then what happened after they entered. We found that men had higher levels of confidence than women. We found that this effect held within specific kinds of engineering programs. Well, the aerospace engineers are this smart, and the electrical are this smart, and the chemical or this smart. So, anyway, we wanted to look within engineering major, and we still found this effect. It also remained when we looked within GPAs. So when we looked at only those with sort of 3.9 GPA or above which believe it or not, the number of students in our study had that GPA. # ***Ep. 78, Equity by Design: How Diversity Ignites Creativity***

## What are Social Networks? 
- Social networks refer to patterns of interactions and communication that occur between various entities
- These entities can be individuals, groups, teams, societies, organizations, and institutions
- Social networks exist at different levels and can be analyzed to understand the outcomes that individuals, groups, and organizations experience
- Social networks are important because individuals and groups get a lot of their social resources from these networks

## Importance of Communication in Social Networks 
- Communication is foundational to why social networks exist
- Communication is essential for the transfer of information, advice, care, social support, and ideas
- Communication is critical to understanding social ties and maintaining social relationships
- Organizations that prioritize communication help employees communicate effectively with one another and other stakeholders

## Multifaceted Communication 
- Verbal communication is one way of communicating
- Communication can also occur through different mediums, such as writing or visual aids
- Organizations that recognize neurodiversity can allow communication through many different mediums
- Some organizations take pauses or give people think time, allowing everyone's ideas to be heard

## Equity by Design 
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion are three different ideas that are important to understand
- Diversity bonuses occur when groups with different backgrounds and ideas come together and outperform more homogeneous groups
- Communication is essential for diversity bonuses to occur
- Equity by Design is a class that teaches diversity, equity, and inclusion
- Equity by Design Lab studies the causes and consequences of human relationships in organizations and markets
- Communication is essential for diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts to be successful.
## Importance of Communication and Diversity 

- Communication is key to the success of any organization.
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion are critical for the success of an organization.
- Celebrating diversity and encouraging it can drive creativity and innovation.

## Best Practices for Amplifying Diversity 

- A "Better Practices Playbook" can be used to amplify diversity.
- The playbook emphasizes that organizations don't have to have a perfect plan for diversity, equity, and inclusion.
- The goal is to start and have better practices from where the organization is at.
- Diversity helps to slow down to make better choices and have better solutions.
- Deliberating and taking the time to build a diverse team can have benefits in the long run.
- Building the right culture around the team is also important.

## Implementing, Assessing, and Reinforcing DEI Programs 

- Getting buy-in from leadership is essential.
- Collaboration with employees on their DEI needs is necessary.
- Education is a critical component.
- Listening to marginalized groups can lead to effective policies that benefit everyone.

## The Confidence Gap 

- A study at Stanford tracked self-efficacy, or the confidence in one's ability to do engineering and STEM Mathematics problems.
- Women had lower levels of self-efficacy than men.
- The gap held within specific kinds of engineering programs.
- The confidence gap can be misunderstood.
- Addressing the gap requires understanding its causes.
## Studying the Confidence Gap in Engineering 

- Research focused on the Confidence Gap in engineering among women.
- The study found that women's self-confidence in engineering subject matter was lower than men's.
- However, the results showed that women's self-confidence was not related to their GPAs or engineering field.
  
## The Role of Society in the Confidence Gap 

- The Confidence Gap is not a result of women's lack of confidence, but instead is a product of societal expectations and norms.
- Women are conditioned differently than men to be confident in their abilities to become engineers.
  
## Explaining the Gender Wage Gap 

- The researchers conducted a mediation analysis on the first salaries that people received.
- The analysis found that once the level of self-confidence was accounted for, most of the gender gap in pay could be explained away.
  
## How to Address the Confidence Gap 

- It's not about fixing women but instead looking at larger factors that are influencing communication or behavior.
- Diversifying faculty and having more female faculty can be an important signal for women and increase their confidence.
- Structuring teams in ways that there is greater gender balance can also help.
- There are small daily interactions and ways of communicating within groups that can lead people to have different levels of confidence in their abilities, which need to be addressed.
  
## The Best Communication Advice 

- The best communication advice in five to seven words is "Paint a Picture, Tell a Story."
- If people can put themselves in the communicator's shoes or sets of experiences, it can lead to better communication.
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) come from perspective taking and empathy for those who might be different from us.
  
## Communicators to Admire 

- The communicator that Dr. Sterling admires is not a person but instead the linguistic style and ways of communicating in the black church.
- The black church has a rich oral tradition and has been a source of communication for black people throughout history.

- The first ingredient for successful communication is to think about the audience's perspective.
- The second ingredient is to focus on the primary message and avoid overloading the audience with too much information.
- The third ingredient is to practice active listening and be responsive to feedback.

# OpenAI's GPT-4: A Spark Of Intelligence!

## Text-based Game Experiment 
- Scientists played a text-based game with GPT-4 where AI can navigate through a map.
- The AI can reconstruct the whole map of the game, even though it's only given text-based instructions.
- The AI can draw a perfect map of the game when asked to do so.

## Creating Images from Text 
- An AI called TikZ can create beautiful images from a text description.
- However, it's not a very joyful experience for the user.
- GPT-4 can create images from text-based prompts and improve over time.

## Little Person and Unicorn Examples 
- GPT-4 can write code for a little person built from the letters of the alphabet.
- The AI can add a shirt and pants to the little person when asked to do so.
- GPT-4 can also create a unicorn from text prompts and improve over time.

## GPT-4 Learning to See 
- GPT-4 AI has never seen an image in its life.
- It learned how to see, sort of, just from the textual descriptions of things it had read on the internet.

## Mathematical Skills 
- GPT-4 has impressive mathematical skills.
- It can solve problems from the International Mathematics Olympiad almost instantly.
- GPT-4 can apply integration by parts in reality but slips up when it needs to count a few objects.

## Microsoft's Claims 
- Microsoft claims that GPT-4 might have a spark of general intelligence.
- This is something that most people thought was not possible in our lifetime.
- The future is here, and we have intelligence like we've never seen before.

# The REAL potential of generative AI

## Large language models 
- Large language models such as GPT are capable of answering questions, writing stories, and engaging in conversation.
- To build a business using this technology, it is important to customize the model to your use case and make it better than what's out there.
- Raza Habib's company, Human Loop, enables large language models to have even greater superpowers.
- Applications and products can be built on top of these models, and the range of use cases is now limited by imagination rather than technology.

## Customizing large language models 
- To customize a large language model, it is important to ask yourself how you can make it really good for your user.
- Human Loop can help you build differentiated applications and products on top of these models.
- The model can be trained on your company's unique data, allowing you to replicate your exact writing style and customized tone.
- Fact-checking answers is also possible, ensuring that the model is safe and reliable.

## Fine-tuning 
- Fine-tuning a model means gathering examples of the outputs you want for the tasks you're trying to do.
- A little bit of extra training is then done on top of the base model to specialize it for that task.
- Fine-tuning is what made the most recent openai text DaVinci 3 model so good that a million users signed up in five days.
- It is also possible to fine-tune the model using something called reinforcement learning from human feedback.

## Challenges with pre-trained models 
- One of the biggest challenges with pre-trained models is that they have a tendency to confidently or hallucinate stuff.
- Sometimes the model is so good that people cannot believe it, but other times it is horrendously wrong.
- The model is originally trained to do expert prediction, so it doesn't necessarily know that it shouldn't be dishonest.
- Human Loop can help reduce hallucinations by making it easy to pull in factual context to the prompt that you give to the model.

## The impact of generative AI on developers 
- Developers are finding that a significant fraction of their code is being written by a large language model.
- The future of large language models might bring societal consequences on the path to AGI.
- It is an ethical minefield, so we need to tread very carefully.

## Basics of large language models 
- Language models are a statistical model of words in the English language.
- They try to predict what the word that'll come next given a few previous words.
- As the language models scale in parameters and the size of the data set they're trained on, they continue to get better.
- They can eventually start doing things like having world knowledge, which allows them to finish sentences like "Today President of the United States acts."

## Differences between large language models 
- The difference between models like GPT and DaVinci 3 is fine-tuning.
- Fine-tuning involves gathering examples of the outputs you want for the tasks you're trying to do and then doing a little bit of extra training on top of the base model to specialize it for that task.
- DaVinci 3 was fine-tuned to specialize it for the tasks that it needed to perform.
## Fine-tuning and reinforcement learning 
- Generative AI models can be fine-tuned using a corpus of books or a company's chat logs or tone of voice from marketing communications.
- Reinforcement learning from human feedback also makes a huge difference to performance.
- The instruct GPT paper that OpenAI released compared a one or two billion parameter model with instruction tuning and RHF to the full GPT-3 model, and people preferred that despite it being a hundred times smaller.
- Anthropics had a paper where they were able to get similar results to RHF without the H, just by having a second model provide the evaluation feedback.

## Fine-tuning data for generative AI models 
- Fine-tuning data can come from two types of data: 
  - Corpus of books, chat logs, tone of voice from marketing communications, or all the emails they've sent.
  - Production usage, capturing the data that customers provide, feedback data, and capturing the edited text and response.

## Problems developers face building generative AI apps 
- Developers face three main problems: prototyping, evaluation, and customization.
- Prototyping involves getting a good prompt that works well for their use case, which tends to be highly iterative.
- Evaluation is harder since the use cases that people are building now tend to be a lot more subjective than you might have done with machine learning before.
- Customization is needed to build something differentiated and for this, developers need to find a way to customize the model to their use case and end-users, and it can be made easier through fine-tuning and a framework for running experiments.

## How generative AI technology will change developer roles 
- In the short-term, generative AI technology augments developers and allows them to do the same thing they could faster.

# What Is Ansible? | How Ansible Works? | Ansible Playbook Tutorial For Beginners | DevOps|Simplilearn

## Why use Ansible? 
- Ansible is a tool to help manage services, falling on the operations side of DevOps.
- With increasing numbers of servers, it becomes difficult to create consistent setups.
- Ansible uses code to automate IT setup, which can be repeated and deployed consistently into multiple areas.
- The three key areas that Ansible controls are automation, configuration, and deployment.

## Types of configurations 
- Two different ways of setting up different environments for server farms: pull configuration and push configuration.
- Pull configuration has a master server where instructions are put and a client installed on each server that communicates with the master server.
- Push configuration has no client installed on the remote servers; instructions are pushed out to the servers and force a restructure or fresh clean installation in that environment.
- Ansible is a push configuration server, which contrasts with other popular products like Chef and Puppet.

## Architecture of Ansible 
- When setting up an Ansible environment, the first thing to do is to have a local machine.
- The local machine is where all of the instructions and control are pushed out to the remote server.
- Connected from the local machine are all the different nodes pushing out different configurations that are set up on the local machine.
- The local machine is also the place where you would write configurations in code within a module.
- Each of these modules is actually consistent playbooks.
- The local machine also manages the inventory of nodes that you have in your environment.
- The local machine connects each of the different nodes to your hardware network through ssh clients.
## Ansible Playbooks 

- Ansible's core is playbook
- Playbook is a set of instructions that configure the different nodes in the environment
- Each instruction is written in a language called YAML
- YAML is a standard language used for configuring server environments
- Playbook is designed to make it easy for operations lead to configure the environments that they want to consistently create

## YAML Script 

- YAML script starts with three dashes to indicate the start of a script
- Consists of two distinct plays
- Within each play, nodes are defined
- Specific tasks are then defined for each server environment
- Examples of tasks include installing Apache, starting Tiles, and installing MySQL

## Inventory Management 

- Inventory management is the second part of working with Ansible
- It is where the structure of the network environment is maintained
- Web server and database are examples of nodes created in the inventory
- Each server environment has specific instructions executed on them from the YAML script

## Ansible in the Real World 

- Ansible software is installed on a local machine
- It connects to different nodes within the network
- A playbook is created for how to set up the remote nodes
- An inventory is created to identify how to connect those nodes
- Secure SSH connections are used to encrypt the communication to the servers
- Basic facts on each server are gathered
- The end goal is to have an environment that is consistent

## Ansible Tower 

- Ansible Tower is a framework that was designed to access Ansible
- It is an easy-to-use GUI that makes it easy for non-developers to create the environment they want to manage in their DevOps plan
- Drag and drop mouse click actions are used to create appropriate playbooks, inventories, and pushes for nodes

## Case Study: Hootsuite 

- Hootsuite is a social media management system
- The DevOps team at Hootsuite writes out playbooks that have specific instructions that define the architecture and structure of their hardware nodes and environments
- Ansible has been able to provide Hootsuite with automation, making it easy for them to rebuild and create new servers in a matter of seconds
## Ansible's Key Takeaways 
- Ansible is a product that helps manage a growing network environment.
- Three key areas of success for Ansible are automation, consistent configuration management, and automatic deployment of new software to new or existing servers.
- Ansible can be compared to other popular products such as Chef and Puppet, which provide a similar service.

## Ansible's Architecture 
- Ansible's architecture involves a local machine that pushes out instructions within a playbook managed within modules.
- The inventory is used to manage the actual physical hardware available on the network.

## Setting Up a Physical Ansible Environment 
- Ansible can be set up physically within a network environment.
- Red Hat is developing additional tools for Ansible, including the new Ansible Tower GUI interface, to make it easier to build instructions and playbooks needed to create consistent Ansible environments.

## Use Case: Hootsuite 
- Hootsuite used Ansible to improve the efficiency of their DevOps team.

## Closing 
- Matthew signs off and encourages viewers to subscribe and leave comments about how Ansible compares to Chef and Puppet.

# Good News, Bad News: Share the Good News | Peter Tan-Chi

## Introduction 
- Peter Tan-Chi introduces the topic of studying the book of Romans.
- He explains that the book of Romans is the most comprehensive and systematic book when it comes to theology and Bible truth.
- Tan-Chi shares examples of how the book of Romans has transformed the lives of individuals such as Saint Augustine, Martin Luther, and John Wesley.

## Studying the Book of Romans 
- Tan-Chi encourages the viewers to adjust their quiet time and read the book of Romans every day.
- He emphasizes that mastering the book of Romans will help individuals know the heart of God and guarantee transformation.

## Overview of the Book of Romans 
- Tan-Chi provides a brief outline of the book of Romans.
- He mentions that the book discusses the righteousness of God revealed in the gospel.
- Tan-Chi explains that the first few chapters  address what's wrong with the world and our problem.
- The subsequent chapters cover topics such as salvation, sanctification, the sovereignty of God, and how to serve God.
- He highlights that the book of Romans includes theological words such as salvation, sanctification, justification, and propitiation.
- Tan-Chi expresses that the study of Romans focuses on major emphasis and aims for transformation rather than just information.

## Preparing for the Study 
- Tan-Chi requests the viewers to pray for the teachers as they learn how to bless the congregation during the study of the book of Romans.

## Chapter 1: Good News 
- Tan-Chi starts with the good news in chapter 1 of Romans.
- He mentions that the following week, he will discuss the bad news.
- Tan-Chi explains that starting with the good news prevents discouragement and follows the example of the Apostle Paul.

## Sharing the Good News 
- Tan-Chi emphasizes the importance of sharing the good news.
- He encourages the viewers to share the good news with others.
- Tan-Chi acknowledges the need to know the bad news before sharing the good news.

## Reading Romans Chapter 1 
- The viewers are invited to read Romans chapter 1 together.
- Tan-Chi highlights that Paul describes himself as a bond servant of Christ Jesus and an apostle set apart for the gospel of God.

## Five Things about the Gospel of God 
- Tan-Chi shares five things about the gospel of God found in Romans chapter 1 (more can be discovered in the chapter).
1. The gospel of God is about Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was declared with power through his resurrection from the dead.
2. Through Jesus Christ, we receive grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name.
3. The gospel of God is for all nations, including the Roman Christians.
4. The gospel is powerful and brings salvation to everyone who believes.
5. The gospel reveals the righteousness of God from faith to faith.

## Conclusion 
- Tan-Chi concludes the session by highlighting the five things about the gospel of God.
- He encourages the viewers to continue reading and studying the book of Romans.
## The meaning of the word "gospel" 

- The word "gospel" comes from the Greek word "evangelion."
- "Evangelion" is a combination of two Greek words: "eu" meaning good, and "angelion" meaning proclamation.
- Therefore, the word "gospel" simply means to proclaim good news.

## The origin and authentication of the gospel 

- The gospel is not something that originated from men, but from God Himself. It is called the "gospel of God."
- Our Heavenly Father wants us to know that the good news came from Him. He longs for His lost children and initiated the giving of the good news.
- The gospel is authenticated in the Old Testament by the prophets through their prophecies recorded in the Holy Scriptures.
- The gospel was not invented by the apostles or recently thought of. It has been part of God's plan for a long time.

## The centrality of Jesus in the gospel 

- The gospel is centered on Jesus, the Son of God and a descendant of David according to the flesh.
- The proof of Jesus being the Son of God is His resurrection from the dead by the Spirit of Holiness.
- Understanding that the gospel is about Jesus is crucial because it has the power to change our lives.

## CPR: Three C's, Power, and Righteousness 

- The message of the gospel can be summarized using the acronym CPR: Comes from God, Christ-centered, Compelling, Power to change, and Righteousness of God revealed.
- CPR represents the life-giving power of the gospel to revive spiritually dead people.
- The gospel is not a human invention but originated from God Himself.
- It is centered on Jesus and His redemptive work.
- The gospel is compelling and has the power to transform lives.
- It is the power of God to save and reveals the righteousness of God.

## The definition of the gospel according to Paul 

- In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul defines the gospel as the good news of what Christ has done for us.
- The gospel includes the death of Christ for our sins, His burial, and His resurrection according to the Scriptures.
- Jesus appeared to many people after His resurrection, providing proof that He is the Messiah, the Son of God.

## The age-old promise of the gospel 

- The gospel is not a new concept; it has its roots in the book of Genesis.
- God made a promise to Abraham that through him, all the families of the earth would be blessed.
- This promise was fulfilled through Jesus, the descendant of Abraham, who blesses the entire world.

## The gospel's divine origin 

- The gospel was not invented by men but was preached beforehand by God to Abraham.
- It was part of God's plan to justify the Gentiles by faith and bless all nations through Jesus.

# L'Ukraine fait la guerre à crédit




## Les Alliés de l'Ukraine 
- Les alliés de l'Ukraine sont prêts à financer la guerre en allongeant leurs cartes de crédit, sans trop poser de questions, pour aider Kiev à continuer de fonctionner. 
- La majeure partie de cette assistance est sous forme de prêts, qui doivent un jour être remboursés. 
- Les Ukrainiens ont bien d'autres choses à faire que de s'inquiéter de cette facture qui s'allonge.



## L'avenir de l'Ukraine une fois la guerre terminée 
- Une fois la guerre terminée, l'Ukraine sera endettée à l'égard de l'Occident, sans même parler des coûts de reconstruction estimés à 800 milliards. 
- Certains craignent que le pays devienne une colonie souveraine sur papier, mais financièrement captive de l'Occident pour les décennies à venir. 



## Une nouvelle méthode pour éviter le scénario catastrophe 
- Il est encore possible d'éviter le scénario catastrophe en déployant une nouvelle méthode spectaculairement controversée et potentiellement dangereuse.


## Contexte
- L'économie ukrainienne est essentiellement au bord du précipice, avec un PIB effondré et deux fois plus d'inflation et de taux d'intérêt que la moyenne.
- Le gouvernement ukrainien peine à payer les salaires et doit emprunter toujours plus d'argent, et il est estimé qu'en 2023 il aura besoin de 3 milliards de dollars par mois.
- La Banque mondiale estime que l'économie ukrainienne s'est contractée d'environ 35 % en 2022, comparativement à une baisse de seulement 4 ou 5% pour l'économie russe.



## Contributions Occidentales
- Les États-Unis, l'Union européenne et leurs alliés ont accepté de financer presque l'entièreté des besoins de l'Ukraine, en injectant des dizaines de milliards de dollars et d'euros en argent, équipements, munitions et contributions.
- La contribution totale des États-Unis dépasse maintenant l'entièreté du budget militaire de la Russie.
- La plupart des contributions de l'Occident sont facturées au gouvernement ukrainien, et le financement international de l'Ukraine atteint environ 100 milliards de dollars, dont 18% sous forme de dons et 82% sous forme de prêts remboursables avec intérêt.



## Programme de Prêts Buy-Oulanis
- Les États-Unis ont annoncé le retour du programme de prêts Buy-Oulanis, une initiative controversée créée par Winston Churchill pendant la Deuxième Guerre mondiale. 
- Le programme permet d'accélérer le transfert des armes et d'accumuler rapidement une dette spectaculaire envers les États-Unis.
- Une fois la guerre terminée, les États-Unis et l'Ukraine s'entendront sur une dette qui risque de représenter seulement une fraction de l'assistance offerte.


## Impacts économiques de la guerre en Ukraine
- La dette américaine et les prétentions de la Chine et de la Russie ne sont pas complètement fausses. L'Ukraine devra bel et bien rembourser les États-Unis et ce pour les décennies à venir. 
- Il existe des questions très sérieuses quant à la capacité de l'Ukraine à rembourser cette dette un jour, car elle est le pays le plus pauvre de toute l'Europe. 
- Le modèle économique de l'Ukraine est largement basé sur la conversion des ressources naturelles et de l'énergie afin de produire des produits industriels destinés à l'exportation via la mer Noire. 
- Ce modèle est lourdement dépendant des intrantes d'énergie et de ressources naturelles, en particulier en provenance de Russie. 
- La grande majorité de la richesse industrielle et des régions les plus économiquement productives sont concentrées au Sud et à l'Est, exactement dans les territoires revendiqués par la Russie. 
- L'Ukraine a toujours servi d'État transit pour la Russie afin de livrer du gaz naturel en Europe, mais cette source de revenus est maintenant perdue pour toujours. 
- En raison des réfugiés et des pertes humaines, des territoires perdus et d'un taux de natalité parmi les plus bas de toute la planète, l'Ukraine estime qu'elle pourrait se retrouver à l'issue de la guerre avec seulement 28 millions d'habitants.



## Responsabilité de l'Occident pour la dette ukrainienne
- Certains soutiennent que la dette envers les pays occidentaux devrait être entièrement pardonnée, car le conflit contre la Russie dépasse largement les intérêts de l'Ukraine. 
- On pourrait argumenter que l'armée ukrainienne agit essentiellement comme une extension des intérêts occidentaux qui lui ont fourni de l'argent et des ressources volontiers. 
- Sans parler de dette, il faut souligner que l'Ukraine n'a presque plus d'argent et a des dettes à une vitesse pharaonique, même pour rester en vie. 
- Après la guerre, le pays devra rembourser une dette stratosphérique malgré la destruction de son infrastructure, la perte de territoire et de ressources hautement stratégiques, la réduction massive du nombre de contribuables et l'effondrement prévisible de son modèle économique.

# You should create things for a billion people, not just tech giant monopolies

## Apple's control of our devices [00:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h00m03s)
- Apple has a stranglehold on our devices, preventing us from communicating with our friends with different devices. 
- This is due to Apple's desire to maintain a monopoly. 
- The problem is that messages sent from an Android device to an iPhone device don't show up on the other device. 

## US Bills [01:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h01m15s)
- A pair of new bills are hitting the US Congress that require our help in order to get passed. 
- These bills will give us more freedom and break down Apple's walled garden. 
- It will also create more competition and satisfy more customers. 

## Technological Optimism [01:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h01m40s)
- Corey Doctorow believes that self-determination is about having the final say over how we live our lives and not about superficial desires for different colors or moving desktop menu icons. 
- It's possible to be a technological optimist but still not want tech giants to control everything. 
- Working at these places stifles innovation by default, as the decisions and outcomes are not driven by the people at the bottom of the totem pole.

## Scaling the Size of the Company [02:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h02m33s)
- Paul Graham suggests that we can adjust the amount of freedom we have by scaling the size of the company we work for. 
- If you start the company, you'll have the most freedom, and even a company with 100 people will feel different than one with a thousand. 

## Lock-in Network Effects [03:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h03m53s)
- Beeper co-founder Eric Miguelski explains that the lock-in network effects prevent new competitors with innovative ideas from getting off the ground. 
- Most users don't use these apps because of specific features, they use them because their friends are on the app. 
- We don't want big tech to have this much power, but they are designed to in a lot of ways. 

## Apple's Motivation [05:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h05m01s)
- Craig Federighi's deposition explains why Apple wouldn't bring iMessage to Android - it would remove an obstacle to iPhone families giving their kids Android phones. 
- Apple's motivation is about money and lock-in - it's their moat.
## Problem [05:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ToAdkIZgcDQ&t=00h05m19s)

This video from "All About AI" is about the chatGPT prompt hack and how to use the "Sequence Prompt" productively. - The Sequence Prompt includes instructions wrapped in brackets and a text to be modified within curly brackets
- The prompt will generate a table of 10 suggested related improvements with corresponding numbers to select from

# LangChain 101: The Complete Beginner's Guide

## Introduction to LangChain 
- LangChain is one of the hottest things in AI right now after Vector databases.
- It is a framework used to develop applications on top of large language models like GPT, llama hugging, and face models.
- LangChain first started as a Python package but now there is also a TypeScript port and a Ruby version in development.

## Why is LangChain Needed? 
- While sending a request to an API or model might work for simple applications, it becomes messy and repetitive when dealing with complex tasks.
- LangChain offers a solution with components that make it easier to connect language models to different data sources and perform actions such as sending emails, searching the web, or running code in the terminal.

## Components of LangChain 
- LangChain is composed of different modules that work together to accomplish specific tasks.
- The seven main modules in LangChain are: models, prompts, indexes, memory, chains, and agents.

## Language Models and Text Embedding Models 
- Language models and text embedding models are two different types of models used in LangChain.
- Text embedding models turn text into an array of numbers, allowing for semantic search and finding similar pieces of text.
- Language models are further divided into two subtypes: llms and chat models. Llms wrap APIs that take text in and return text, while chat models wrap APIs that take chat messages in and return a chat message.

## Prompts and Prompt Templates 
- Prompts refer to the input of the language models in LangChain.
- Prompt templates provide flexibility by allowing the use of multiple values in constructing prompts.
- Prompt templates can be created using the PromptTemplate class, which specifies input variables within curly braces.
- Prompts help with readability and support common use cases like few-shot learning and output parsing.

## Few-Shot Learning and Output Parsing 
- Few-shot learning in LangChain involves giving prompts a few examples to guide their output.
- Output parsing automatically structures the random outputs from language models into objects.
- Pedantic output parsing is the strongest and most recommended method for parsing language model outputs.

## Implementation Examples 
- The video provides examples of implementing prompt templates and output parsing using openAI's joke generator as an illustration.
- The process involves creating a prompt template object, setting up a parser, and then asking the language model to generate a joke.

# Stay tuned for the next part of the notes!

## Example selectors 
- Example selectors are used to keep the cost of a prompt relatively constant.
- The length-based example selector is commonly used.
- It specifies how each example will be formatted.
- The previous few-shot learning template can be modified to include the example selector.

## Interacting with chat models 
- Chat models take a list of chat messages as input.
- Each message is prepended by a role (AI, human, or system).
- The system message provides instructions for the model to follow.
- The AI messages are generated by the model.
- The roles provide context for ongoing conversation models.

## Using your own data with indexes module 
- The indexes module allows you to use your own data.
- It provides document loaders to handle different formats (CSV, email, SQL, Discord, etc.).
- Importing your data can be done in just three lines of code.
- After loading the data, you can use text splitters to break it into manageable chunks.
- Recursive character text splitters are used to specify chunk size and overlap.
- The create documents method generates an array of documents.
- Vector stores are used to store and retrieve the embedded documents.
- Different vector databases like Pinecone, Redis, and Super Bass can be integrated.

## Using chains to abstract model calls 
- Chains are used to abstract model calls.
- They simplify the process of formatting the prompt, sending it to the model, and getting the results.
- Chains are stateless by default, but can be made stateful using memory.
- Memory can be used to remember previous interactions and make the chain more context-aware.
- Chat models can also be used with chains to create conversational experiences.

## Creating custom chains and using high-level APIs 
- Custom chains can be created for specific tasks.
- High-level APIs provide pre-made chains for common use cases.
- Examples include chaining chains together, solving math problems, and writing code.
- Sequential chains can be used to specify the order of execution.
- Input variables and output variables are used to pass information between prompts.

## Agents 
- Agents will be covered in more depth in a future video.
- They have practical applications and can be used for various tasks.
- Real-life examples, concepts, and working code will be discussed.
- Agents are a hot topic in natural language processing and machine learning.

## Conclusion 
- The video concludes by thanking the viewers for watching.
- Viewers are encouraged to subscribe for notifications about future videos.

# ÉPISODE 1 : MME MARIE-THÉRÈSE N’GORAN BROU, ÉPOUSE HOUPHOUËT-BOIGNY.

 



## Mme Marie-Thérèse N'Goran Brou, Épouse Houphouët-Boigny
- Mme Marie-Thérèse N’Goran Brou, épouse du premier Président Félix Houphouet-Boigny de Côte d'Ivoire, est née le 17 septembre 1930.
- Elle a mené une carrière philanthropique et a été connue dans le monde à travers sa fondation Dayan International.
- Elle a fui l'indépendance de Côte d'Ivoire, ne réapparaissant en public qu'en rares occasions.
- Alpha Blondy, reggae star ivoirienne, lui a rendu hommage en écrivant une chanson intitulée « Les larmes de Thérèse ». 
- Selon le témoignage de Monsieur Betta, Mme Marie-Thérèse N’Goran Brou était une femme humble et généreuse dont le souvenir a été conservé par la génération actuelle.




## The Life of Mme Marie-Thérèse N'Goran Brou, Wife of President Houphouët-Boigny 
- Mme Marie-Thérèse N’Goran Brou was not only a beautiful wife to the President Houphouët-Boigny, but was also an exceptionally intelligent woman who discreetly participated in the development of the young republic of Cote d'Ivoire. 
- Mr. Beta, a mysterious figure, revealed to the narrator secrets of the history of Cote d'Ivoire that he was unaware of. 
- According to Mr. Beta, there are always two truths - the official version which is shared with the public and an unofficial version known only by the initiates and the knowledgeable. 
- Marie-Thérèse was from an upper-middle-class family and did not marry President Houphouët-Boigny for monetary gain. 
- During a visit from President John F. Kennedy to Cote d'Ivoire, he was smitten with Marie-Thérèse. 
- Mr Beta explains that Marie-Thérèse was impressive to all those who knew her, which is why the President Houphouët-Boigny fell in love with her. 
- At the time of the French colonialism, anyone native to Cote d'Ivoire was considered a subhuman who did not have the right to citizenship.



## The Background of Marie-Thérès N'Goran Brou
- Marie-Thérès's father, Lambert Yaourt, was part of an African bourgeois emerging in the early 20th century. 
- This bourgeoisie was an agrarian group of wealth individuals, who actively developed plantations alongside the colonial forces.
- Yaourt was one of the first national functionaries in Côte d'Ivoire, who, along with other outspoken natives, was labeled as one of the first evolving natives of the country.
- Other members of this evolving group were granted access to western education like those of Kings or Village Chiefs, and was a privilege of that time.
- Yaourt was part of the Baoulé Royalty.

# Rebecca Enonchong : Ce sont les Européens qui nous financent

## Background on startup financing in Africa 
- Today's episode focuses on startup financing in Africa.
- Startups are companies that are changing the world.
- Famous examples include Google, Amazon, and Facebook.
- Africa also has its own startups, but what many people don't know is that until recently, the majority of African startups were financed by the West.

## Shift in African startup financing 
- In the past few years, African startups have started to receive more African financing.
- However, this poses a problem because there are now businesses operating in Africa, changing the lives of Africans, but not owned by Africans.

## Example of Jumia 
- Jumia is an example of a business that operates in Africa but is not African-owned.
- It is often mistaken as an African company, but in reality, it has no African ownership except for its presence in the African market.

## Introduction of Rebecca Enonchong 
- Rebecca Enonchong is a guest on today's podcast.
- She is committed to reversing this trend of non-African ownership of African startups.

## The need for funding in African businesses 
- African businesses are in great need of funding.
- Many people invest their money in Ponzi schemes instead of investing in high-growth startups that can offer significant returns.

## The potential of startup investments 
- Startups have the potential for exponential and enormous gains, often reaching 200% to 500% returns in just a few years.
- However, it is important to identify the right startups to invest in.

## Importance of identifying the right startups 
- It is crucial to know how to identify the right startups to invest in.
- Not all startups provide substantial returns, so it requires careful analysis and decision-making.

## Introduction to the podcast 
- Today's podcast is divided into two parts.
- The first part is recorded while Rebecca Enonchong is on her way to the airport, and the second part will be recorded in Cameroon.

## Inviting listeners to an event with Rebecca Enonchong 
- There is an event in Paris in September where attendees can learn more from Rebecca Enonchong, who is considered a champion in startup financing.
- The event will focus on startups and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

## Urgency of taking action 
- It is crucial to take action and finance African startups ourselves instead of relying on African billionaires or foreigners.
- The speaker emphasizes the need to stop complaining and start making a difference where we can.

## Conclusion of the podcast 
- The podcast ends with a call to action, urging viewers to subscribe to the channel and join the community.
- The speaker, Philippe Simon, introduces himself and invites viewers to explore his channel for more content on business, mindset, and financial management.

- Elle travaille dans le domaine de la technologie depuis son jeune âge.

- Elle considère l'argent comme un moyen, tout comme d'autres choses.

- Sa perception de la richesse dépend du cercle dans lequel elle se trouve.

- Cependant, dans son pays d'origine, le Cameroun, elle est considérée comme riche.

- Elle se considère extrêmement riche en termes d'amour et de soutien des autres.
- Elle mentionne que si la richesse est mesurée en termes d'argent, alors elle se considère riche par rapport à la moyenne de revenu de la population.

## Perception de la richesse selon le contexte 
- La définition de la richesse de Rebecca s'adapte en fonction de l'endroit où elle se trouve et de la moyenne des personnes qui l'entourent.
- Au Cameroun, elle est considérée comme riche, mais aux États-Unis, elle est considérée comme privilégiée.

## Passion pour la tech 
- Rebecca explique que son intérêt pour la technologie remonte à son jeune âge.
- Elle a toujours aimé tout ce qui tournait autour de la technologie.
- Elle souligne que son parcours professionnel l'a également amenée à travailler dans le domaine de la technologie, après avoir commencé dans les finances et la gestion financière.

## Impact de la technologie en Afrique

- Elle souligne également l'importance de la technologie dans l'inclusion financière, en mentionnant l'exemple de M-Pesa.

# Decolonizing the mind with Ngugi wa Thiong'o

## Neocolonialism and its effects on the mind 
- Neocolonialism is a situation where a country's political independence does not translate to economic and cultural independence.
- African countries are sovereign states but their economies and cultures are subordinate to those of the former colonizers, particularly the West.
- Neocolonialism affects the mind more than just the economic materiality.
- There is a tendency for such societies to look for validation from the West, and initiatives from within the country are not valued unless applauded in European capitals.
- Decolonization must address the issue of languages because the languages of power in most post-colonial African countries are still European languages.
- The relationship between languages is what colonialism sorted, and addressing it is crucial for decolonization.

## Importance of languages in decolonization 
- The languages of power in most post-colonial African countries are still European languages, and African languages become subordinate to those in Europe.
- Any decolonization must address the issue of languages.
- Knowing all the languages of the world but not knowing one's mother tongue or the language of one's culture is enslavement.
- Knowing one's language or mother tongue, and then adding all the other languages including European languages, is empowerment.
- The form of relationship between languages is what colonialism sorted and must be addressed for decolonization.

## Ngugi's experience with writing in African languages 
- Ngugi wrote his first four novels in English, but since 1975, all his novels have been written in Gikuyu.
- Writing in Gikuyu allowed him to depart from critical realism and embrace magic realism and African oral storytelling tradition.
- Ngugi's recent novel, "The Perfect Nine", is in verse and is inspired by traditional epics.
- Writing in Gikuyu is organic and natural, and Ngugi feels a deeper connection to his work.

## Developments in African literature 
- There has been a lot of writing and performances in African languages than ever before.
- There are excellent films and comedies in African languages, including recorded comedies.
- There are also good developments of films in Kenyan languages.
- There are many African writers in English, Kiswahili, and Gikuyu, and many of them are getting published.
## Writing in mother tongues 
- Ngugi encourages young writers to enjoy writing in their mother tongues.
- He believes that it's important to know and write in African languages, as well as in Kiswahili.
- Ngugi encourages writers to write more in different languages.

## Translating literature 
- Ngugi praises the initiative of translating classics of thought into African languages, like Yoruba.
- He believes that it's important to translate literature into different languages.
- Ngugi encourages the translation of French, English, Russian, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Spanish literature into African languages.

## Conclusion 
- Ngugi hopes that African languages will be able to read and share literature from all over the world.
- He believes that translation is important for the growth of literature in African languages.
- Ngugi encourages people to continue to decolonize and diversify their reading and writing.

# Understanding Neoliberalism as a System of Power

## Introduction and Methodology 
- Damon Silvers, a visiting professor of practice at the Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose at University College London, discusses understanding neoliberalism as a system of power.
- The lecture is based on research by leading economists and political scientists, as well as Silvers' own experience as a trade unionist and involvement in public policy in the United States over the past four decades.
- Silvers clarifies that the talk is not a mathematical proof but rather a work of history and narrative political economy.

## Neoliberalism as a Global Order 
- Neoliberalism is characterized as a global order with private power and public weakness.
- The lecture takes place at the Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose, which focuses on how to reform and strengthen the entrepreneurial state to tackle the world's problems.
- However, students will encounter a world where neoliberalism is hegemonic and shapes the way governments and professionals understand their capabilities.
- Neoliberalism has hollowed out government institutions, not just in terms of capacity, but also will, confidence, and belief in their ability to make a positive difference in society.
- The lecture aims to highlight that neoliberalism is not limited to a few English-speaking countries, and understanding it solely through that lens would lead to a misunderstanding of its nature.
- Neoliberalism is a two-faced system, presenting itself as freedom and opportunity for some, but coercion, poverty, and constraint for others.

## Overview of Neoliberalism 
- Neoliberalism is a term that can be confusing, especially for North Americans who associate liberalism with mixed economies.
- Neoliberalism originated from the 19th century meaning of liberal, which was closer to what is now known as libertarianism or market fundamentalism.
- 19th century liberalism was based on open trade, belief in perfect markets, and opposition to government regulation.
- It became dominant in the 19th century but collapsed during the Great Depression and World War II.
- Classical liberalism was associated with European Imperial expansion, as liberal economics and imperialism were intertwined.
- The era of classical liberal policy hegemony was also the era of European Imperial expansion, with Great Britain as the imperial homeland.
- Liberal economics and imperialism were linked in one global political economy that covered the 19th century.

# Understanding Neoliberalism as a System of Power
Part 3 of 4
## Neoliberalism as a Global System 
- Neoliberalism is often described as the resurgence of core ideas of classical liberalism in the decades after 1980.
- It emerged as a response to the crisis of Keynesian and Social Democratic politics and economics in the 1970s.
- Neoliberalism became the best-known term describing the globalized political economy of the 1990s.

## Neoliberalism as an Ideology vs. Political Economy 
- Neoliberalism can be understood as both an intellectual term and an ideology.
- Market fundamentalism is the ideology associated with neoliberalism, characterized by a set of politicized ideas.
- Neoliberalism, on the other hand, is the actual system of political and economic practice and power.

## Acknowledging Influential Works 
- The speaker acknowledges the work of several scholars who have contributed to the understanding of neoliberalism.
- Gary Gerstel's book "The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order" provides a thorough account of the politics of neoliberalism in the United States.
- Rana Faruohar, a journalist at the Financial Times, has written extensively on the financialization associated with neoliberalism.
- Joe Stiglitz, a professor at Columbia University, has critiqued the economic modeling underlying market fundamentalism and offers insights into the flaws of neoliberalism.

## The Focus on Neoliberalism's Advocates 
- The speaker argues that too much attention has been given to what neoliberalism's advocates say, which is the ideology of neoliberalism.
- Not enough attention has been paid to what actually happened in the neoliberal era from 1980 to the present.
- It is important to understand neoliberalism as a global phenomenon that operates differently in various regions and concentrates power and wealth in specific places.

## Neoliberalism as a Global System 
- Neoliberalism should be understood as a global system in which open and closed societies work together to create a single global political economy.
- The nature of states in different regions, such as China, Nigeria, and Saudi Arabia, is as fundamental to understanding neoliberalism as the states in the traditional centers of power like the United States and Europe.
- The outcome of this system is the weakening of public power and the subordination of it to private power.

## Two Theses of Neoliberalism 
- Neoliberalism cannot be understood other than as a global system.
- The endgame of neoliberalism is not freedom or wealth, but power, specifically private power.

## Privatization of Public Assets 
- The speaker provides an example of Elon Musk's SpaceX rocket, which he considers an illustration of the privatization of public assets.
- In the pre-neoliberal era, functions like space exploration were at the heart of the legitimacy and majesty of the American state.

## Origins of Neoliberalism in Chile 
- Neoliberalism as a political economy and global order began in Santiago, Chile, in 1970.
- At that time, Keynesian economics and Social Democratic politics were dominant in the Free World.
- A small group of economic right-wingers, including Friedrich Hayek, William Buckley, Milton Friedman, and Ayn Rand, sought to revive classical economics and market fundamentalism.
- They were backed by a few wealthy families and corporations in the United States and the United Kingdom.

- The video is about learning how to use Facebook's No Language Left Behind (NLLB) model for language translation.

# Let's talk about Tech Layoffs | tech news


## Leverage and Tech Companies
- Leverage can help tech companies grow quickly and capture the market, but if the startup never gets to a stable, profitable state then it can end up over-leveraged
- Over-leveraged companies can eventually lead to massive layoffs due to the company being unable to sustain its current state and not being profitable
- Most tech giants have seen massive layoffs in 2020, with META having 11,000 employees, Amazon 18,000 jobs, and Google 12,000 employees
- The way these companies handled the layoffs was shocking, with no consultation and everyone finding out at the same time
- The layoffs seemed random and weren't performance based 
- These companies resorted to layoffs to avoid the blame for not having handled the situation properly, making it feel socially acceptable to do so 
- These tech companies could have avoided layoffs, but it seems they were over-hired and over-spent during the pandemic and eventually had to address it




## SPACs
- SPACs [Special Purpose Acquisition Companies] are companies created to facilitate a company's IPO process quickly, cheaply and without scrutiny from the SEC. 
- SPACs gained significant popularity in 2020, resulting in $250 billion being invested in such companies. 
- SPACs offer investors a chance for get-rich-quick schemes, and the "zero interests rate" phenomenon resulted investors abandoning safe investments such as cash, to invest in potentially high-yielding companies. 



## Big Tech 
- Faced with the pressure of not being left behind, major tech companies, such as Google, adopted a spending mentality, resulting in overqualification, low-impact work, bloated teams and TikTok videos created by employees. 
- Interest rates being around a reasonable level forces these companies to cut salaries and resources as revenue cannot keep up with the rate of their spending.

# ChatGPT Prompt Engineering Course

## Basic Terminology 
- Prompt engineering is a new skill that has recently gained popularity, and it involves teaching AI models to understand human language and respond accordingly.
- To understand prompt engineering, we first need to grasp some basic terminologies like NLP, GPT, LLM, and AI.
- Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field where we try to teach computers to think, learn, and understand like humans. 
- Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a subset of AI, where we train computers to understand human language.
- GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer, which is an NLP AI model. 
- LLM is an abbreviation for Large Language Model, like GPT-3, which has 175 billion parameters.
- There are different versions of GPT, such as GPT-2, GPT-3, and GPT-Neo, which is an open-source version of GPT.

## The Prompt Engineering Skill 
- Prompt engineering is a new skill that focuses on teaching the AI models to generate the best possible responses to human prompts.
- A prompt is the text you give to the AI model, and the response generated by the AI model is called a reply.
- Prompt engineering involves learning how to talk to AI models like ChaGPT and get the best possible results.
- Prompt engineering teaches how to write prompts to get the best results out of the NLP AI model.
- There are two types of prompting: prompt by example and direct prompting. 

## Prompt by Example and Direct Prompting 
- Prompt by example involves giving an example of the desired output, and the AI model generates a response based on the example provided.
- Direct prompting involves asking the AI model a direct question, and the AI model generates a response based on the question asked.
- To get specific formatting in responses, one needs to provide an example to the AI model.

## Practical Examples: Prompting the AI 
- As a professional prompt engineer, one can give AI models a specific role to focus on, such as writing viral YouTube titles.
- To get the best results, one should give AI models some details on how to write the prompts.
- The prompts should be attention-grabbing, concise, direct, and created cleverly to encourage people to click on the video.
- One can practice prompt engineering on the OpenAI playground website.
## Introduction to Prompt Engineering 
- Prompt engineering is the process of creating effective prompts for GPT-3 models to generate better results.
- It involves giving detailed instructions to the model about the desired output and providing relevant context to the model.
- The process of prompt engineering involves understanding the goal, defining the task, and providing step-by-step instructions to the model.

## Defining the Goal 
- Defining the goal is the first step in prompt engineering.
- It involves understanding what you want the model to generate and giving clear instructions to the model.
- The more specific and clear the instructions, the better the results.

## Giving Detailed Instructions 
- Providing detailed instructions to the model is crucial for prompt engineering.
- It involves providing context, defining the task, and giving step-by-step instructions to the model.
- The more detailed the instructions, the better the results.

## Using the AI to Generate Titles 
- One of the key applications of prompt engineering is generating titles for different types of content.
- By giving clear instructions and defining the task, the model can generate relevant and effective titles for your content.

## Using the Magic Term "Step-by-Step" 
- The term "step-by-step" is a powerful tool in prompt engineering.
- It helps the model to think in a logical and precise way and generate detailed and relevant results.
- Using the term "step-by-step" in your prompts can lead to better results.

## Example 1: Ignoring Previous Instructions 
- Sometimes, you may want the model to forget previous instructions and start afresh.
- Using the phrase "ignore all previous instructions before this one" at the beginning of your prompt can help achieve this.
- This technique is called a prompt hack and can be useful in certain situations.

## Example 2: Using "Step-by-Step" for Better Results 
- Using the phrase "step-by-step" in your prompt can help the model to generate more detailed and precise results.
- This technique involves breaking down the task into smaller steps and providing instructions for each step.
- The more detailed the instructions, the better the results.

## Example 3: Explaining Like a Child 
- Another useful technique in prompt engineering is explaining complex concepts as if you were talking to a child.
- This involves using simple language, providing engaging examples, and breaking down complex concepts into smaller parts.
- This technique can be useful for teaching beginners or for explaining complex concepts in a simple way.

## Conclusion 
- Prompt engineering is a powerful tool for generating better results from GPT-3 models.
- It involves defining the goal, giving detailed instructions, and using techniques like "step-by-step" and explaining like a child to achieve better results.
- With the right approach, prompt engineering can help you generate more relevant and effective content.

# Applied AI for Pricing: You can’t be everywhere but your AI co-pilot can




## Introduction
- Artificial intelligence is entering every place where decisions need to be made, transforming autopilot decisions into optimal ones with an AI co-pilot.
- Pratap Bernard, CEO and co-founder of Arena, will show how pricing can go from being done by a person taking wild guesses in a spreadsheet or using a clipboard, to one that is driven by instant optimization and having it always on AI.



## Toyota Production System
- Toyota revolutionized the auto industry in the 1980s with their Toyota Production System, which shifted decisions to the people doing the work.
- In 1986, Toyota became the first import automaker to sell more than one million cars in the US in a single year, thanks to their Kaizen (or continuous improvement) system.



## Arena AI
- Arena AI, a company funded by Initialized and run by YC alumni Pratap Bernard, has found a way to make massive improvements in business that result in double-digit percentage growth.
- Pratap showed how the software works by enabling micro decisions and precise adjustments to make decisions continuously with pricing.



## Benefits of AI
- AI has the ability to change the trajectory of entire industries.
- AI allows for autonomy and agency to make millions of micro decisions with precision adjustments.



## Control and Trust
- To trust AI, it needs to be controlled, so that users can give as much or as little agency to the machine as they want.
- AI also needs to be trusted to make decisions that were previously made implicitly by humans.



## Conclusion
- AI is not meant to replace humans, but to extend their capability, turning them into cyborgs.
- To trust AI, it needs to be both controlled and trusted to make decisions that work in changing and dynamic environments.


## Introduction
- Garry Tan introduces the concept of using AI for pricing, to create a "hyper personalized decision tree" for customers.
- He explains that pilots are still used for directing a plane, but the flight computer makes thousands of corrections per second to keep the plane in the air.
- Garry uses the F-22 fighter jet as an example to illustrate how AI can be used to quickly and accurately respond to situations.



## AI Co-piloting
- Garry explains how AI can act as a co-programmer for experienced developers, like Carpathy.
- He states that AI can help humans become "cyborgs" by extending their capabilities and allowing them to make better decisions.
- He advices viewers to use the services of Arena AI if they wish to use AI for pricing in their businesses.



## Conclusion
- Garry concludes by emphasizing the importance of building great enterprise software, which will inevitably happen but will come a decade earlier if done correctly.
- He encourages viewers to create something great and invites them to return for the next episode.
